slides.title: We reproduced RL-driven improvement at small scale.
slides.notes:
We practiced a published RL method on math before applying it to RLMs. On the same 64 questions, correct answers rose from 20 to 47. The chart keeps every check, including the last dip.

This reproduces improvement at small scale, not the full benchmark result. Training is stopped; checkpoints are saved.

Next: what made learning possible?

slides.title: Useful practice is neither all wrong nor all right.
slides.notes:
Walk through x = 4 versus x = 5. We compare attempts on the SAME question. All wrong or all right gives this method no relative reward signal. A mix gives it a useful contrast.

A curriculum could keep practice within reach, then raise the difficulty. Mixing easy and impossible questions is not enough.

Next: can the model use its existing skills?

slides.title: Existing skill needs a usable interface.
slides.notes:
Point to the starting scores: 154 versus 305 out of 500. Same model, different way of asking. A poor interface can hide ability and make the training gain look larger.

Knowing Python is not the same as knowing our RLM tool interface or choosing useful subtasks. Demonstrations may help; SFT is not always needed.

Next: what should we teach first?

slides.title: Teach the interface, then practice useful choices.
slides.notes:
Tell the invented example: Mira works at Aster Lab; Aster Lab is in Oxford. The second lookup needs the employer's name. Calling a helper is not enough: it needs useful context.

Teach missing skills, then practice linking them. More attempts may reveal rare successes, but can repeat the same mistake.

This sequence is a hypothesis to test.

slides.title: Prior work supports the ingredients, not our sequence.
slides.notes:
These ingredients have precedents. DAPO keeps informative reward groups. RLM work uses demonstrations. R1 adds supervised preparation; R1-Zero shows it is not always required.

None establishes our proposed teaching order. Our question is which preparation helps RLMs learn and combine skills on new tasks.

Next: small experiments to distinguish ideas.

slides.title: A portfolio of small experiments, not one settled story.
slides.notes:
Start by locating the failure: tool use, passing context, choosing a plan, or using feedback. Each suggests a different small test.

Compare staged versus shuffled examples; more attempts at the same total cost; success-only versus repair demonstrations. Keep helper models fixed and test new combinations.

Close: prepare learnable tasks, then test what helps.
